code:
A table with 40 fields, 15 rarely populated:
- every row carries that width, every read
- every indexed field adds write overhead
  on every insert and update, forever

Invisible at 500 test records.
Very visible at 10 million production records.
caption: Field count and table width have a direct cost on query performance.

steps.label: Extend task
steps.sub: the data genuinely is a kind of task; you accept the shared table gets wider

steps.label: Build new
steps.sub: the data doesn't semantically belong there, or you want to isolate its growth

steps.label: Either way
steps.sub: the wrong call is expensive to undo once reports and integrations depend on it

code:
At design time, ask:
'What does this table look like after 8 years
 of real production use?'

Prefer reference fields over free text for
categorical data. Resist 'just in case' fields.
Design around how the table will actually
be queried, before it's built.
caption: A design that's fine at a thousand records can fail at ten million.

subtitle: Keeping years of accumulated data from degrading the tables you just designed.
